blocks.robotComment: Taxes get a bad reputation, but understanding them well is one of the highest-leverage things you can do for your money. 📋
blocks.body: Taxes are money collected by a government, generally from income, purchases, or property, used to fund public services: roads, schools, emergency services, defense, and countless other things that a society funds collectively rather than individually. Almost every country has some form of income tax, and the specific rules vary enormously from place to place.

This track focuses on the ideas behind how taxes generally work — the concepts that show up in some form almost everywhere — rather than any one country's exact rules, which change often and vary by location. The goal is to leave you able to read your own country's specific tax rules with real understanding, not to memorize a list of numbers that may not even apply to you.

highlights.text: the ideas behind how taxes generally work

blocks.sentence: Taxes are generally used to fund ___ that a society funds collectively rather than individually.
options: public services
private companies
personal savings accounts
blocks.explanation: Roads, schools, and emergency services are classic examples of things funded collectively through taxes rather than paid for individually.

blocks.robotComment: This track deliberately teaches concepts, not country-specific numbers — those change, the underlying logic doesn't. 🌍
blocks.body: Because tax rules genuinely differ by country, this track is intentionally generic: it explains how income tax concepts generally work, using illustrative numbers rather than any real country's actual brackets or rates. When it's time to actually file your own taxes, you'll want your own country's current, official information — but the concepts here will make that information far easier to understand.

blocks.question: Why does this track use illustrative, generic numbers instead of one specific country's real tax brackets?
options: Tax rules vary enormously by country and change often, so generic concepts stay accurate longer than specific numbers would
Real tax numbers are considered private information
No country actually publishes its tax rates
Illustrative numbers are always higher than real ones
blocks.explanation: Concepts like marginal rates and deductions show up almost everywhere in some form, even though the exact numbers differ by country and change over time.

blocks.statement: Almost every country has some form of income tax, though the specific rules vary a lot by location.
blocks.explanation: Income tax is nearly universal in some form, but brackets, rates, deductions, and filing rules differ significantly from country to country.

blocks.robotComment: The number in your job offer and the number that actually hits your bank account are rarely the same. Here's why. 💸
blocks.body: Gross income is the full amount you earn before anything is taken out: your stated salary, or the total of an hourly wage times hours worked. Net income, sometimes called take-home pay, is what's actually deposited into your bank account after taxes and other deductions are subtracted.

The gap between the two is generally made up of income tax withheld, and often other deductions too: retirement contributions, health insurance premiums, and other benefits, depending on where you live and work. This is exactly why a $60,000 salary doesn't mean $60,000 shows up in your account over the year.

code.code:
Gross income:        $60,000
Minus taxes/deductions: −$14,000  (illustrative)

Net income (take-home): $46,000
code.caption: The exact gap varies enormously by country, income level, and personal choices like retirement contributions — this is just illustrative.

blocks.sentence: The amount actually deposited into your account after taxes and deductions are subtracted is called ___ income.
options: net
gross
total
blocks.explanation: Net income (take-home pay) is what's left after gross income has taxes and other deductions subtracted from it.

blocks.robotComment: Budgeting off your gross salary is a common first-job mistake — always plan around net. 🎯
blocks.body: This distinction matters most when budgeting: a common early-career mistake is planning a budget around gross salary, then being surprised that far less actually arrives. Every budget, including the ones covered in the Money Basics track, should be built around net income, since that's the number that's actually available to spend or save.

blocks.question: Why should a personal budget be built around net income rather than gross income?
options: Net income is what's actually available to spend or save, after taxes and deductions are already taken out
Gross income is always smaller than net income
Net income never changes throughout the year
Budgeting only matters for gross income
blocks.explanation: Gross income was never fully available to begin with — net income is the real number that shows up in your account.

blocks.statement: Net income is generally the same number as gross income.
blocks.explanation: Net income is gross income minus taxes and other deductions — the two are almost always different amounts.

blocks.robotComment: This is probably the single most misunderstood idea in personal finance. Let's fix that. 🧠
blocks.body: Many countries use a progressive tax system, where the tax rate increases as income increases. But the common misconception is that earning more can suddenly tax your entire income at a higher rate. That's not how it actually works — a progressive system taxes different slices of your income at different rates, not your whole income at one single rate.

highlights.text: different slices of your income at different rates

blocks.body: Here's a simplified, illustrative example (not real rates from any country): imagine income up to $20,000 is taxed at 10%, the next slice from $20,000 to $50,000 is taxed at 20%, and anything above $50,000 is taxed at 30%. Someone earning $60,000 doesn't pay 30% on the whole $60,000 — they pay 10% on the first $20,000, 20% on the next $30,000, and 30% only on the last $10,000.

code.caption: Only the portion of income inside each bracket is taxed at that bracket's rate — never the whole income at the top rate.

blocks.sentence: In a progressive tax system, different ___ of income are taxed at different rates, not the entire income at one rate.
options: slices
years
accounts
blocks.explanation: Each bracket only taxes the portion of income that actually falls inside it, which is the core idea behind a progressive system.

blocks.question: In the illustrative example above, why doesn't someone earning $60,000 pay 30% on the entire $60,000?
options: Because only the portion of income above $50,000 falls into the 30% bracket — the rest is taxed at the lower bracket rates
Because $60,000 doesn't count as taxable income
Because tax brackets only apply to income under $20,000
Because the 30% rate only applies to self-employed people
blocks.explanation: Progressive systems tax each slice of income at that slice's own rate — the higher rate only ever applies to the portion above the threshold.

blocks.statement: A raise that pushes part of your income into a higher tax bracket means your entire income suddenly gets taxed at that higher rate.
blocks.explanation: Only the portion of income that falls inside the higher bracket is taxed at that bracket's rate — this is the exact misconception this lesson debunks.

lessons.title: What a Tax Bracket Actually Means

blocks.robotComment: Level 1 introduced progressive systems in general — now let's zoom into the actual mechanism. 🔍
blocks.body: A tax bracket is simply a range of income taxed at a particular rate. A progressive tax system is built out of several of these ranges stacked on top of each other, each one starting where the previous one ends. The bracket itself isn't a rate applied to a person — it's a rate applied to a specific slice of income.

highlights.text: a range of income taxed at a particular rate

blocks.body: Here's a fresh illustrative example, with different numbers than Level 1 used, just to show the same idea holds no matter what the specific figures are. Imagine a system with four brackets: 10% on income up to $15,000, 20% on income from $15,000 to $45,000, 30% on income from $45,000 to $100,000, and 37% on anything above $100,000.

code.code:
Illustrative bracket structure (not real rates from any country):
  10% on $0 – $15,000
  20% on $15,000 – $45,000
  30% on $45,000 – $100,000
  37% above $100,000
code.caption: Each bracket only ever taxes the slice of income that falls inside its own range.

blocks.sentence: A tax bracket is a range of income taxed at a particular ___.
options: rate
year
account
blocks.explanation: A bracket defines both a range of income and the rate that applies specifically to the portion of income inside that range.

blocks.robotComment: The boundary number is a threshold, not a cliff edge — nothing bad happens right at the line. 🚧
blocks.body: The dollar amounts separating brackets, like $15,000 or $45,000 in the example above, are called bracket thresholds. Crossing a threshold doesn't change how the income below it is taxed — it just means any additional income earned past that point starts being taxed at the next bracket's rate.

blocks.question: In the illustrative four-bracket example above, what happens to income between $45,000 and $100,000?
options: It falls inside the 30% bracket and is taxed at 30%
It is taxed at 37%, the highest bracket
It is not taxed at all
It is taxed at 10%, the lowest bracket
blocks.explanation: That specific slice of income, from $45,000 up to $100,000, falls inside the 30% bracket and is taxed at that bracket's rate.

blocks.statement: A tax bracket applies a single rate to a person's entire income, rather than to a specific slice of it.
blocks.explanation: A bracket applies its rate only to the slice of income that falls within its range — that's the whole mechanism behind a progressive system.

blocks.body: Keep this bracket structure in mind, since the next lesson uses it to directly debunk one of the most persistent myths in personal finance: the idea that earning more money can somehow leave you with less.

highlights.text: debunk one of the most persistent myths

blocks.robotComment: Level 1 debunked this once already — it's worth debunking again with a raise instead of a starting salary, since that's where the myth usually strikes. 🎯
blocks.body: Here's the misconception, stated plainly: some people believe that if a raise pushes their income into a higher tax bracket, their take-home pay could actually go down. It cannot. Only the portion of income that falls inside the new, higher bracket is ever taxed at that bracket's rate — everything below it keeps being taxed exactly as before.

Using the bracket structure from the last lesson, imagine someone earning $95,000 gets a $10,000 raise, bringing them to $105,000. That crosses the $100,000 threshold into the 37% bracket. A worried reaction might be: doesn't that mean all $105,000 now gets taxed at 37%? It doesn't — only the $5,000 above $100,000 is taxed at 37%.

highlights.text: only the $5,000 above $100,000 is taxed at 37%

code.caption: Take-home pay rose by $6,650 on a $10,000 raise — less than the full raise, but never a decrease.

blocks.sentence: A raise that pushes part of your income into a higher bracket can reduce how much of the raise you keep, but it can never make your total take-home pay ___.
options: decrease
increase
disappear
blocks.explanation: Only the new, higher slice of income is taxed at the higher rate — every dollar of a raise still adds at least some amount to take-home pay.

blocks.question: In the worked example, why did take-home pay rise by $6,650 instead of the full $10,000 raise?
options: Because $5,000 of the raise fell into a higher bracket and was taxed at a higher rate, while still being fully kept minus that tax
Because the entire $105,000 was taxed at 37%
Because raises are taxed twice
Because the worker actually earned less than before
blocks.explanation: The portion of the raise in the new bracket is taxed at a higher rate than the rest of the income, which is why the after-tax gain is smaller than the raise itself — but still a real gain.

blocks.statement: In the example, the worker's take-home pay after the raise was still higher than before the raise.
blocks.explanation: $79,150 in take-home pay after the raise is higher than the $72,500 before it — a raise into a higher bracket is never a pay cut.

blocks.robotComment: If you ever hear someone turn down a raise to "avoid a higher bracket," you now know exactly why that reasoning doesn't hold up. 💬
blocks.body: This is precisely why turning down a raise, or extra freelance work, out of fear of a higher bracket almost never makes mathematical sense. The new bracket only ever applies to the new income above the threshold, and that new income, even taxed at a higher rate, still adds to what you keep.

highlights.text: still adds to what you keep

lessons.title: Effective Tax Rate vs. Marginal Rate

blocks.robotComment: Two different numbers, both called "your tax rate" in casual conversation — here's how to tell them apart. 📐
blocks.body: Your marginal tax rate is the rate applied to your last dollar of income — the bracket you're currently sitting in. Your effective tax rate is different: it's your total tax bill divided by your total income, which gives you the average rate you actually paid across every dollar you earned.

Because a progressive system taxes lower slices of income at lower rates, your effective rate is always lower than or equal to your marginal rate, unless there's only one bracket in play. Using the worker from the last lesson, who earned $105,000 and paid $25,850 in total tax, their marginal rate is 37%, but their effective rate is much lower.

highlights.text: always lower than or equal to your marginal rate

code.code:
Income: $105,000
Total tax: $25,850
Marginal rate: 37%  (the rate on the last dollar earned)

Effective rate = total tax / total income
              = $25,850 / $105,000
              = about 24.6%
code.caption: Only the top slice of income was taxed at 37% — the average rate paid across all income was far lower.

blocks.sentence: Your ___ tax rate is your total tax bill divided by your total income.
options: effective
marginal
flat
blocks.explanation: The effective rate is an average across all your income, while the marginal rate is the rate on just your last dollar earned.

blocks.question: Why is the effective tax rate almost always lower than the marginal tax rate in a progressive system?
options: Because lower slices of income are taxed at lower rates, pulling the average below the top rate
Because the effective rate is calculated incorrectly on purpose
Because the marginal rate only applies to people with no income
Because effective rate and marginal rate always describe the same number
blocks.explanation: Since only the top slice of income is taxed at the marginal rate, and every lower slice is taxed at a lower rate, the blended average — the effective rate — comes in below the marginal rate.

blocks.statement: Someone's marginal tax rate and effective tax rate are usually the exact same number under a progressive system.
blocks.explanation: The marginal rate only applies to the last slice of income, while the effective rate blends every bracket a person's income passed through — they're almost always different.

blocks.robotComment: This is exactly why headlines about "the top tax bracket" can sound scarier than what people actually pay. 📰
blocks.body: This distinction matters for how you think about your own finances: your marginal rate is the right number to use when estimating the tax impact of one more dollar of income (like a raise or bonus), while your effective rate is the right number to use when thinking about your overall tax burden as a share of everything you earned.

highlights.text: marginal rate is the right number
effective rate is the right number

questions.question: What is a tax bracket?
options: A range of income taxed at a particular rate
A single fixed tax amount everyone pays
A type of bank account
A country's total tax revenue

questions.statement: The dollar amounts separating tax brackets are called bracket thresholds.

questions.sentence: Crossing a bracket threshold means only the income above it is taxed at the ___ bracket's rate.
options: next
first
average

options: Still increase their total take-home pay, just not by the full raise amount
Always decrease their total take-home pay

questions.statement: Turning down a raise to avoid a higher tax bracket generally makes mathematical sense.

blocks.robotComment: Not all income is created equal in the eyes of a tax system — here's the first big split. 🧩
blocks.body: Earned income is money you receive in exchange for work: a salary, hourly wages, tips, or profit from running your own business. It's the kind of income most people think of first, and it's usually what the bracket examples so far in this level have been describing.

Other income covers money that comes from sources besides your labor. Investment income is a major category here: dividends paid by companies you own shares in, interest paid on savings or bonds, and capital gains, which is profit from selling an investment for more than you paid for it. Rental income from property you own is another common example.

blocks.sentence: Money received in exchange for work, like a salary or wages, is called ___ income.
options: earned
passive
deferred
blocks.explanation: Earned income specifically refers to income from labor — a job, wages, tips, or self-employment.

blocks.robotComment: Same word, different meaning depending on when it's used — worth locking in early. 🔑
blocks.body: Profit from selling an investment is specifically called a capital gain, and it only exists as taxable income at the point of selling — simply watching an investment grow in value while you continue holding it doesn't create a capital gain by itself. This distinction becomes important later in this track and elsewhere in personal finance.

blocks.question: Which of these is the clearest example of earned income?
options: Wages paid for hours worked at a job
Dividends paid on shares of stock
Interest paid on a savings account
Profit from selling a rental property
blocks.explanation: Wages are paid directly in exchange for labor, which is exactly what defines earned income.

blocks.statement: An investment simply growing in value while you continue to hold it automatically creates taxable capital gains that year.
blocks.explanation: A capital gain generally only becomes real, taxable income once the investment is actually sold — unrealized growth on paper is not the same thing.

blocks.body: This split between earned income and other income sets up the next lesson's question directly: why would a tax system ever treat these two categories differently, rather than just adding everything into one pile and taxing it the same way?

lessons.title: Why Different Income Types Can Be Taxed Differently

blocks.robotComment: Tax policy is never just about raising money — it's also a set of incentives baked into a rulebook. 🎛️
blocks.body: In many tax systems, earned income and certain kinds of other income, especially long-term capital gains, are taxed under different rate structures. This isn't random: governments often use the tax code to encourage or discourage particular behaviors, not just to collect revenue.

A common policy reason is encouraging long-term investment: many systems tax profit from an investment held for a long time at a lower rate than profit from one sold quickly, to discourage short-term speculation and encourage patient, long-term ownership. Another common reason is that certain payroll-style taxes, which fund specific programs, are sometimes applied only to earned income and not to investment income.

blocks.sentence: Many tax systems tax long-held investment profit at a lower rate than quickly-sold investment profit, partly to encourage long-term, patient ___.
options: ownership
spending
borrowing
blocks.explanation: Favoring longer holding periods is a common policy tool meant to reduce short-term speculation and encourage stable, long-term investing.

blocks.robotComment: The mechanics differ everywhere, but the pattern — using rates as a nudge — repeats constantly. 🌍
blocks.body: The exact mechanics of how earned income and other income are taxed differently vary enormously by country, and some countries barely distinguish between them at all. The important concept to take away isn't a specific rule, but the general pattern: tax rates aren't only about revenue, they're also a tool policymakers use to nudge financial behavior in a particular direction.

highlights.text: a tool policymakers use to nudge financial behavior

blocks.question: What's a common policy reason some systems tax long-term investment gains differently than earned income?
options: To encourage long-term, patient investing over short-term speculation
Because investment income is illegal to tax at the same rate
Because investment income is always smaller than earned income
Because only wealthy people earn any investment income at all
blocks.explanation: Favoring longer holding periods with a different rate structure is a common way tax codes try to shape financial behavior, not just collect revenue.

blocks.statement: Every country in the world taxes earned income and investment income under identical rate structures.
blocks.explanation: The exact rules vary enormously by country — some distinguish sharply between income types, others barely distinguish at all.

blocks.body: With both income types and the reasoning behind treating them differently in view, the next lesson pulls everything from this level together into one illustrative person's full financial picture.

highlights.text: one illustrative person's full financial picture

lessons.title: A Simple Example Pulling It Together

blocks.robotComment: Time to put brackets, marginal vs. effective rate, and income types all in one place. 🧮
blocks.body: Meet an illustrative person: they earn $80,000 in salary from their job (earned income), plus $4,000 in dividends and interest from investments (other income) over the year, for $84,000 in total income. Using this level's bracket structure — 10% to $15,000, 20% to $45,000, 30% to $100,000, 37% above $100,000 — all of it falls under $100,000, so no income reaches the 37% bracket.

To keep this example simple, imagine this illustrative system taxes both income types the same way, using the same brackets — remember, some real systems draw a distinction here, but plenty of the underlying logic works the same either way. Here's the full calculation.

code.code:
Total income: $84,000  ($80,000 salary + $4,000 investment income)

Tax owed:
  10% x $15,000 = $1,500
  20% x $30,000 = $6,000
  30% x $39,000 = $11,700
  --------------------------
  Total tax = $19,200

Marginal rate: 30%  (the rate on the last dollar earned)
Effective rate = $19,200 / $84,000 = about 22.9%
Take-home: $84,000 - $19,200 = $64,800
code.caption: One combined picture: total income, total tax, marginal rate, effective rate, and take-home, all in one place.

blocks.sentence: In the example, the illustrative person's marginal rate was 30% while their effective rate was about ___%.
blocks.explanation: The 30% marginal rate only applied to the top slice of income — blended across all $84,000, the effective rate worked out to about 22.9%.

blocks.question: Why didn't any of this illustrative person's income get taxed at the 37% bracket?
options: Because their total income of $84,000 never crossed the $100,000 threshold where that bracket begins
Because investment income is never taxed
Because salary is always exempt from the top bracket
Because the 37% bracket doesn't apply to anyone
blocks.explanation: The 37% bracket only applies to income above $100,000, and this person's combined income stayed below that threshold.

blocks.statement: In this example, the $4,000 of investment income was simply added to total income before applying the brackets.
blocks.explanation: To keep the example simple, both income types were combined and taxed under the same bracket structure.

blocks.robotComment: Notice how every idea from this level — brackets, the misconception, effective vs. marginal, income types — just showed up in one worked example. That's the whole point of this lesson. 🧷
blocks.body: Every concept from this level shows up in this one example: brackets determining how each slice is taxed, a marginal rate that's higher than the effective rate actually paid, and two different income types combining into one total. That's the real skill this level builds: being able to look at any income picture and reason through what's actually happening, rather than guessing.
